raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old Pakistani male presented to the hospital with diarrhea and progressively worsening fatigue for ten days. Diarrhea was watery and did not contain any blood. He also complained of decreased appetite, pain while passing urine, and a reduction in the amount of urine for five days. There was no history of fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cough, skin rashes, or altered sensorium. The patient had no sick contacts and no history of eating food from outside. The patient was a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus for two years, was stabilized on metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and was not taking any other medication. He had a recent history of travel to Pakistan, and his symptoms developed during his return flight to Qatar.
On physical examination, the patient was febrile (38  C) and tachycardiac (104 beats per minute) with normal blood pressure and respiratory rate. The rest of the physical examination was non-significant.
Initial laboratory workup revealed pancytopenia, raised C-reactive protein (CRP), deranged liver enzymes, and elevated creatinine (830) (Table 1). Urinalysis did not show any significant blood cells or casts. Further workup revealed raised creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin, giving an impression of rhabdomyolysis (Table 1). There was no proteinuria, making diabetic nephropathy unlikely. An ultrasound of the urinary tract revealed bulky kidneys with normal echogenicity, with no features of chronic kidney injury or obstruction. Fluid resuscitation was initiated considering pre-renal AKI. The patient was also empirically started on intravenous (IV) Ceftriaxone 2 g daily, given the possibility of an infectious trigger. The stool sample was negative for Clostridium Difficile toxin, ova, or parasites. There was no bacterial growth in urine and stool samples; however, blood cultures grew Salmonella Typhi. Given his recent travel to Pakistan, antimicrobial coverage was escalated to renal adjusted dose of Meropenem (0.5 g every 12 h), considering the possibility of a resistant strain. Subsequently, the sensitivity results revealed a multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi (including ceftriaxone and azithromycin).
Over the next days, the patient's creatinine kept rising (Fig. 1), and he became oliguric. His symptoms had mildly improved with a reduction in diarrhea frequency and improvement in his appetite. On day 3, hemodialysis (HD) was initiated due to persistent oliguria and worsening renal parameters despite fluid resuscitation. The patient underwent 4 HD sessions over the next ten days with remarkable creatinine improvement (Fig. 1). On day seven, the patient began to produce urine, which reached up to 2 L per day by day 10. Creatinine normalized by day ten, and repeated blood cultures came negative. The patient took antimicrobials for 14 days (including one day of ceftriaxone and 13 days of meropenem) and was subsequently discharged asymptomatic with normal renal function.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old Pakistani male presented with a 10-day history of watery non-bloody diarrhea and progressive fatigue, and a 5-day history of dysuria, oliguria, and anorexia after returning from travel to Pakistan.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient's symptoms began during his return flight from Pakistan to Qatar 10 days prior to admission with watery, non-bloody diarrhea and progressively worsening fatigue. Five days before presentation, he developed decreased appetite, pain on urination, and markedly reduced urine output.
subjective.past_medical_history: 2-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled on oral metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. Recent travel to Pakistan; denied sick contacts or eating food from outside vendors.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 10-day watery non-bloody diarrhea, progressive fatigue, anorexia, dysuria, and 5-day oliguria. Pertinent negatives: no subjective history of fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cough, skin rash, or altered sensorium. Home medication: metformin 1,000 mg twice daily.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was febrile (temperature 38 °C) and tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats/min) with normal blood pressure and respiratory rate. The remainder of the systemic physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood work revealed pancytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein, deranged liver enzymes, severe acute kidney injury with serum creatinine 830 µmol/L, and markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin consistent with rhabdomyolysis. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria, hematuria, or cellular casts. Stool testing was negative for Clostridium difficile toxin, ova, and parasites, and urine and stool bacterial cultures showed no growth. Urinary tract ultrasound demonstrated bulky kidneys with normal cortical echogenicity and no hydronephrosis or chronic renal changes.
objective.advanced_workup: Blood cultures grew multidrug-resistant (extensively drug-resistant) Salmonella Typhi with demonstrated resistance to both ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Multidrug/extensively drug-resistant Salmonella Typhi bacteremia (resistant to ceftriaxone and azithromycin) complicated by rhabdomyolysis and severe oliguric acute kidney injury, confirmed by blood culture with susceptibility testing and elevated CK/myoglobin. Clostridioides difficile colitis, intestinal parasitism, obstructive uropathy, and diabetic nephropathy were ruled out. Initial IV fluid resuscitation and 1 day of empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g daily) were escalated to renal-adjusted intravenous meropenem (0.5 g every 12 hours for 13 days; 14 days total antimicrobial therapy), and he underwent 4 sessions of intermittent hemodialysis between hospital days 3 and 10 for persistent oliguria and rising creatinine. Urine output recovered by day 7 (reaching 2 L/day by day 10), serum creatinine normalized, repeat blood cultures cleared, and he was discharged asymptomatic with normal renal function.
